title: Nondisjunction in meiosis I and meiosis II

stimulus.title: Where did the extra chromosome come from?
stimulus.text: Meiosis normally gives each human egg or sperm one copy of each of the 23 kinds of chromosome. Sometimes a pair of chromosomes, or two sister chromatids, fail to separate. A child with Down syndrome has three copies of chromosome 21. Researchers compared a stretch of DNA near the centromere of chromosome 21, where crossing over almost never happens, in the child and both parents. The mother's two copies of chromosome 21 carry different versions of this stretch (types 3 and 4); the father's carry types 1 and 2. The child carries types 1, 3 and 3.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Describe what separates in anaphase I and what separates in anaphase II of normal meiosis.

rubric.point: Describes that homologous chromosomes (the two members of each pair) separate in anaphase I, and sister chromatids separate in anaphase II.
accept: homologs separate in meiosis I, sister chromatids in meiosis II
anaphase I splits the homologous pairs; anaphase II splits each chromosome's two chromatids

parts.sample: In anaphase I the two homologous chromosomes of each pair separate and move to opposite poles, while each chromosome's sister chromatids stay joined. In anaphase II the sister chromatids of each chromosome separate.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why nondisjunction of one chromosome pair in meiosis I makes all four gametes abnormal, while nondisjunction in meiosis II makes only two of the four abnormal.

rubric.point: Explains that a meiosis I error leaves both cells after meiosis I abnormal (one with both homologs, one with none), and meiosis II passes that to all four gametes (two n + 1, two n − 1); a meiosis II error affects only the division of one of the two cells, so the other cell's two gametes are normal (one n + 1, one n − 1, two n).
accept: after a meiosis I error both daughter cells are wrong, so all four products are; in meiosis II only one cell's division fails
MI: 2 with an extra copy and 2 missing it; MII: 1 extra, 1 missing, 2 normal, because the other cell divides normally

parts.sample: If a pair fails to separate in meiosis I, one of the two cells gets both homologs and the other gets none, so both cells are abnormal. Each then divides in meiosis II, giving two gametes with an extra copy (n + 1) and two with no copy (n − 1). If the error happens in meiosis II, meiosis I was normal, so it affects the division of only one of the two cells: that cell gives one n + 1 and one n − 1 gamete, while the other cell divides normally and gives two normal gametes.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Using the DNA types, identify the parent and the division (meiosis I or meiosis II) in which nondisjunction produced this child, and justify your answer.

rubric.point: Identifies the mother, meiosis II, and justifies: the child got one type from the father (1) and two identical maternal types (3 and 3); two identical copies near the centromere are sister chromatids that failed to separate, which happens in meiosis II (a meiosis I error would give one of each of her homologs, types 3 and 4).
accept: mother, meiosis II, because the egg carried two copies of type 3, which are sister chromatids
the egg had 3 and 3, not 3 and 4, so the homologs separated normally and the sisters did not
maternal MII nondisjunction: identical copies near the centromere

parts.sample: The error was in the mother's meiosis II. The child has one copy from the father (type 1), so the sperm was normal, and two copies of type 3 from the mother. If her homologs had failed to separate in meiosis I, the egg would carry one of each (3 and 4). Two identical type 3 copies near the centromere, where crossing over almost never changes the type, are sister chromatids, which separate in meiosis II, so that is the division that failed.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: A gamete missing chromosome 21 (n − 1) is fertilized by a normal gamete. Predict the number of chromosomes in the zygote, and explain why an embryo with one copy of an autosome rarely survives.

rubric.point: Predicts 45 chromosomes (monosomy 21) and explains that one copy of every gene on that chromosome, instead of two, changes the amounts of many gene-made proteins at once, which disrupts development so the embryo usually dies early.
accept: 45; half the normal dose of hundreds of genes upsets development
45 chromosomes, monosomy; too little product from many genes at once is usually lethal
2n − 1 = 45; losing a whole chromosome's worth of gene copies disrupts many processes

parts.sample: The zygote will have 22 + 23 = 45 chromosomes, with one copy of chromosome 21 (monosomy 21). Each chromosome carries hundreds of genes, so the embryo has one copy of all of them instead of two. The amounts of many proteins made from those genes change at once, which disrupts development, so such embryos usually die very early.
